claims.text: The baseline is a FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating deposited without carbon addition.
Magnetron sputtering at substrate temperatures below 400 K produces a nanostructured or amorphous FeNiCrCoCu matrix.
Approximately 5 at.% carbon is introduced into FeNiCrCoCu during co-sputter deposition.
A controlled high-temperature annealing regime can maintain carbon in a supersaturated, finely dispersed state while preventing carbide formation.
Carbon addition produces a supersaturated solid solution containing dispersed carbon clusters.
Dispersed carbon clusters pin grain boundaries in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Carbon-induced grain-boundary pinning refines and stabilizes the coating nanostructure.
Carbon incorporation impedes grain-boundary mobility and inhibits coarsening during high-temperature deformation.
The stabilized nanostructure reduces grain-boundary sliding.
The stabilized nanostructure reduces dislocation mobility.
Reduced grain-boundary sliding and dislocation mobility lower the overall high-temperature wear rate.
Relative to the carbon-free baseline, the carbon-doped and annealed coating will have increased hardness at approximately 400 °C.
Relative to the carbon-free baseline, the carbon-doped and annealed coating will have a significantly reduced wear rate at approximately 400 °C under high normal load.
TEM will show refined grains and finely dispersed carbon features at grain boundaries in the modified coating.
The successfully modified coating will contain no deleterious carbide phases detectable by the proposed phase analysis.
Excessive carbon segregation or unwanted carbide formation may prevent the expected wear-resistance improvement.
